where: Section 2, bullet 'Access from one side only; the beam can even pass through a glass window'
problem: Stated as a general property of laser welding, but it holds only for the 1 µm beams (Nd:YAG, fibre). A CO₂ beam at 10.6 µm is absorbed by ordinary glass and cannot pass through a window, so a student may wrongly generalise it.
fix: 'Access from one side only; a 1 µm fibre-laser beam can even pass through a glass window (a CO₂ beam cannot, because glass absorbs 10.6 µm light).'

where: Section 3, opening of the CMT explanation: 'In ordinary MIG the wire is fed forward at a steady speed and the arc runs at high current. When the wire touches the pool, a short circuit forms...'
problem: This describes only short-circuiting (dip) transfer MIG. Ordinary MIG can also run in spray or globular transfer with no short circuits at all, so the sentence as written is not true of 'ordinary MIG' in general.
fix: 'In short-circuiting (dip) MIG the wire is fed forward at a steady speed and the arc runs at high current. When the wire touches the pool, a short circuit forms...' — say clearly that CMT is a modified short-circuit transfer, not a modification of every MIG mode.

problem: Heat input H = P/v is used without being defined anywhere, and no efficiency factor is mentioned, so the student cannot tell why the number is 'heat input' rather than just 'energy per unit length of travel'.
fix: State the formula before using it: H = P/v, where H is heat input in J/mm, P is power in W and v is travel speed in mm/s; add that P here is the power delivered to the work (arc/laser efficiency is neglected), so the comparison is on a like-for-like basis.
